1.title: Discovery, Communication and Expectations
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: Discovery, Communication and Expectations. This module covers discovery, communication and expectations. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Structured discovery: questions, stakeholders, requirements. How to communicate architecture decisions and trade-offs to different audiences. Expectation management: honest limits, S L A s (service level agreement), S L O s. Feedback loops with stakeholders.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Runs Discovery for an Airline's Disruption Assistant
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Runs Discovery for an Airline's Disruption Assistant. The airline wants an assistant to rebook passengers during disruptions. Operations, legal, customer care, I T security and the C F O each want different things.

1.title: Structured Discovery
1.text: Structured Discovery. The figure shows this: A discovery map: business sponsors, process owners, data owners, risk and compliance, technology and security, and operations, each answering a different question.

1.title: Structured Discovery, continued
1.text: Structured Discovery, continued. Business value. Questions: What outcome, for whom, worth what? What happens if we do nothing? Output: Goals, pillars, targets (Module one). Process and users. Questions: How is the work done today? Who touches it? Where are the pain points and volumes? Output: Process map, personas, baselines. Data. Questions: What data exists, where, how clean, who owns it, how sensitive? Output: Data inventory, access rules. Systems. Questions: Which systems to integrate; A P I s (application programming interface), auth, limits? Output: Integration list, constraints. Risk and compliance. Questions: Which regulations, policies, audit needs; what failures are unacceptable? Output: Risk register, regimes (Module fourteen).

1.title: Structured Discovery, continued
1.text: Structured Discovery, continued. Quality. Questions: How will we know it works? Examples of good and bad outputs? Output: Eval dataset seeds, acceptance criteria. Non-functional. Questions: Latency, availability, scale, cost ceiling. Output: Target S L O s, budget. Operations. Questions: Who runs it, supports it, owns prompts and knowledge? Output: R A C I, runbook outline. Practices. Interview every stakeholder group, not only the sponsor; ask for real examples (tickets, documents, edge cases). Separate needs from solutions: "faster rebooking", not "an agent". Prioritize requirements (must, should, could) and record assumptions and open questions with owners. Run a thin prototype early to turn opinions into evidence.

1.title: Structured Discovery, continued
1.text: Structured Discovery, continued. Capture constraints that shape the architecture: data residency, platform standards, skills, timelines. Exam tip: Good discovery gathers measurable outcomes, real examples, data and risk constraints from all stakeholder groups before any design commitment.

1.title: Communicating Decisions and Trade-offs
1.text: Communicating Decisions and Trade-offs. The figure shows this: Tailoring the message: executives want value, risk and cost; engineers want design and interfaces; security and legal want data flows and controls; operators want runbooks and limits.

1.title: Communicating Decisions and Trade-offs, continued
1.text: Communicating Decisions and Trade-offs, continued. Executives. Needs: Outcome, cost, risk, timeline, decision needed. Format: One-page summary, options with a recommendation. Engineers. Needs: Components, interfaces, patterns, test strategy. Format: Architecture diagrams, A D R s, A P I specs. Security, legal, compliance. Needs: Data flows, controls, retention, residency. Format: Data-flow diagram, control mapping, D P I A inputs. Operators and support. Needs: How to run, monitor, escalate. Format: Runbooks, dashboards, limits. End users. Needs: What it does, what it does not, how to get help. Format: Plain-language guidance, disclosure. Presenting a decision. State the decision and the problem it solves. Show options (at least two or three) with criteria (cost, latency, accuracy, risk, effort). Give a recommendation and the trade-offs accepted.

1.title: Communicating Decisions and Trade-offs, continued
1.text: Communicating Decisions and Trade-offs, continued. List assumptions, risks and mitigations, and what would change the decision. Record it as an architecture decision record (A D R). Quantify trade-offs with evaluation results and measured cost and latency, not adjectives. Be honest about limits: Claude can be wrong, outputs need validation, knowledge has a cutoff, quality is probabilistic, behavior can change with model versions. Do not promise perfect accuracy, zero risk or fixed outcomes; give ranges and confidence.

1.title: SLAs, SLOs and Expectation Alignment
1.text: S L A s, S L O s and Expectation Alignment. S L A. Meaning: Commitment to a customer, often contractual. L L M (large language model)-specific notes: Promise only what the system and dependencies can deliver. S L O. Meaning: Internal target that supports the S L A. L L M-specific notes: Set for latency (p ninety-five), availability, quality (eval score), cost. S L I. Meaning: The measured indicator. L L M-specific notes: Time to first token, error rate, faithfulness rate, escalation rate. Error budget. Meaning: Allowed shortfall. L L M-specific notes: Governs release pace. An S L A for an L L M system depends on platform availability, rate limits, capacity and model behavior; plan retries with backoff, fallbacks (another model or platform, cached answers, human handoff) and capacity (rate-limit tiers, batch for non-urgent work).

1.title: SLAs, SLOs and Expectation Alignment, continued
1.text: S L A s, S L O s and Expectation Alignment, continued. Separate performance S L A s (speed, uptime) from quality targets (accuracy), because quality is statistical: specify it as percent on a defined test set and sampled production, not "always correct". Human review time counts toward end-to-end S L A s. Align expectations early: demos use curated inputs; share the eval set and failure examples.

1.title: Feedback Loops
1.text: Feedback Loops. The figure shows this: Stakeholder feedback loop: pilot, collect feedback and metrics, review in a regular forum, prioritize, release, communicate what changed. Channels: in-product thumbs and comments, reviewer overrides, support tickets, steering reviews, metric dashboards. Regular cadence: a review forum with sponsors, operators and risk. Triage feedback into categories (prompt, retrieval, data, tool, U X, policy) and prioritize by impact.

1.title: Feedback Loops, continued
1.text: Feedback Loops, continued. Close the loop: tell stakeholders what changed and why; add feedback cases to the eval set. Manage scope: new requests get impact analysis (cost, risk, latency) before acceptance. Exam tip: Run discovery with all stakeholder groups, ask for real examples, and separate needs from solutions. Exam tip: Quality is statistical: write S L A s as measurable targets on a test set, never as "always correct".

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Discovery: Business value, process, data, systems, risk, quality, non-functional, operations. Method: All stakeholder groups; real examples; needs not solutions; assumptions logged; thin prototype. Message: Tailor to audience; options, recommendation, trade-offs, assumptions, A D R. Honesty: Probabilistic quality; limits; no absolute promises. S L A or S L O or S L I: Commitment or target or measurement; p ninety-five latency, availability, quality on test set. Resilience: Backoff, fallbacks, capacity, human handoff. Feedback: Collect, triage, prioritize, release, communicate, add to evals.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A sponsor says "just build an agent." What is the best discovery response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Discovery separates needs from solutions and produces testable requirements.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which stakeholder group is most likely to be missed in early discovery and cause late surprises? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Late discovery of regulatory or security constraints forces redesign.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An executive asks for a recommendation among three architectures. How should the architect present it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Executives need options, a recommendation, risks and a decision.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A client demands "one hundred percent accuracy" in an S L A for an L L M assistant. What should the architect do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Set honest, measurable quality targets rather than absolute promises.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two are valid components of a performance S L O for an interactive assistant? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Performance objectives are measurable operational indicators such as p ninety-five latency and error rate, not promises about every answer.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. What should be included when documenting a major design decision? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. An architecture decision record captures the context, options, decision and trade-offs so future teams understand the reasoning.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which design supports an availability S L A when the model platform is occasionally rate-limited? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Resilience patterns protect the S L A against dependency limits.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Stakeholder feedback arrives in tickets, comments and reviewer overrides. What should the team do with it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A closed loop turns feedback into improvements and trust.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. A demo with curated inputs impressed the sponsor, who now expects the same quality on all production traffic. What should the architect do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Sharing evaluation results and failure examples resets expectations with evidence about real performance instead of a curated demo.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. A new feature request arrives mid-project. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. An impact analysis on cost, risk, latency and schedule lets stakeholders prioritize the request without breaking commitments.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: B. Question two: C. Question three: D. Question four: B. Question five: A and C. Question six: D. Question seven: B. Question eight: A. Question nine: A. Question ten: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
